name: Lena Vasquez-Osei
description: Lena Vasquez-Osei is a solo artist from Meridian 88's Circuit District 4, a former assembly-line quality technician who began performing in worker pubs and transit-hub bars in 2207 and never entirely stopped doing the day job until 2213. Her sound is rooted in what Circuit audiences call 'floor music' — unhurried, acoustic-forward compositions that borrow from Andean charango traditions, West African griot storytelling structures, and the melancholic drone of Finnish joik, filtered through a voice that critics have consistently failed to categorize beyond 'necessary.' She plays a modified twelve-string with a piezo pickup feeding a small analog processor she built herself; no neural feed, no BCI augmentation, a choice she is vocal about.
creator: Lena Vasquez-Osei
audience: Circuit workers, mid-tier families, labor union social halls, anyone who finds neural-feed music 'too loud inside your skull' — her words
cultural_impact: Vasquez-Osei occupies a rare position in Meridian 88's music landscape: she is beloved without being commodified, at least not yet. Her 2215 album 'What the Shift Foreman Doesn't Hear' sold forty thousand physical copies in the Circuit before Vantablack's distribution arm noticed and offered a licensing deal she accepted under terms that kept her masters. Circuit residents play her records at funerals, at births, and at the end of long strikes. She is frequently cited by Tier 3 listeners as 'the artist I put on when I need to remember I'm a person,' a phrase that has become something of a cultural shorthand for her entire catalog.
known_fans: Tier 3 mid-managers who grew up in the Circuit and haven't forgotten it
Shelf listeners who find her music through contraband physical copies
story_hooks: Lena Vasquez-Osei has agreed to perform a benefit concert for families displaced by a Shelf flooding event, but the venue — a Circuit transit hub — has just been leased to a Vantablack subsidiary, and the new corporate management wants her to sign a one-night licensing agreement that would give them ownership of the live recording.

A Circuit worker who helped Lena record her first album on a borrowed rig has been arrested on charges that feel manufactured; Lena is quietly asking people she trusts to look into it, unwilling to go public until she knows more.

Someone is distributing a deepfake neural-feed of Lena Vasquez-Osei's voice singing what sounds like a Vantablack Media corporate anthem — the fake is good enough that Circuit communities are fracturing over whether it's real, and Lena herself is refusing to address it publicly for reasons she won't explain.
